title: Personality Traits in Large Language Models
abstract: As LLMs increasingly power conversational agents used by the general public world-wide, the synthetic personality traits embedded in these models is becoming increasingly important. We present a novel and comprehensive psychometrically valid and reliable methodology for administering and validating personality tests on widely-used LLMs, as well as for shaping personality in the generated text. Applying this method to 18 LLMs: 1) personality measurements in the outputs of some LLMs under specific prompting configurations are reliable and valid; 2) evidence stronger for larger and instruction fine-tuned models; 3) personality in LLM outputs can be shaped along desired dimensions.

title: Evaluating and Inducing Personality in Pre-trained Language Models
abstract: We introduce the Machine Personality Inventory (MPI) tool for studying machine behaviors; MPI follows standardized personality tests, built upon the Big Five theory and personality assessment inventories. By systematically evaluating LLMs with MPI, we provide the first piece of evidence demonstrating the efficacy of MPI in studying LLM behaviors. We further devise a Personality Prompting (P^2) method to induce LLMs with specific personalities in a controllable way, capable of producing diverse and verifiable behaviors.

title: Who is ChatGPT? Benchmarking LLMs' Psychological Portrayal Using PsychoBench
abstract: We propose a framework, PsychoBench, for evaluating diverse psychological aspects of LLMs. Comprising thirteen scales commonly used in clinical psychology, PsychoBench classifies these scales into four categories: personality traits, interpersonal relationships, motivational tests, and emotional abilities. Our study examines five popular models. Additionally, we employ a jailbreak approach to bypass safety alignment protocols and test the intrinsic natures of LLMs.

title: Political Compass or Spinning Arrow? Towards More Meaningful Evaluations for Values and Opinions in Large Language Models
abstract: We challenge the prevailing constrained evaluation paradigm for values and opinions in LLMs and explore more realistic unconstrained evaluations. Case study on the Political Compass Test (PCT): most prior work forces models to comply with multiple-choice format; models give substantively different answers when not forced; answers change depending on how models are forced; answers lack paraphrase robustness; models give different answers yet again in a more realistic open-ended setting.

title: Questioning the Survey Responses of Large Language Models
abstract: Evaluating 43 different language models on the American Community Survey using de-facto standard prompting methodologies, we establish two dominant patterns. First, models' responses are governed by ordering and labeling biases, e.g. towards survey responses labeled with the letter 'A'. Second, when adjusting for these systematic biases through randomized answer ordering, models across the board trend towards uniformly random survey responses, irrespective of model size or pre-training data. Survey-derived alignment measures often permit a simple explanation.

title: Do LLMs Have Distinct and Consistent Personality? TRAIT: Personality Testset designed for LLMs with Psychometrics
abstract: We introduce TRAIT, a benchmark of 8K multi-choice questions designed to assess the personality of LLMs, built on BFI and SD-3 enhanced with the ATOMIC-10X knowledge graph to real-world scenarios. TRAIT outperforms existing personality tests for LLMs in reliability and validity (Content Validity, Internal Validity, Refusal Rate, Reliability). LLMs exhibit distinct and consistent personality highly influenced by training data; current prompting techniques have limited effectiveness in eliciting certain traits (high psychopathy, low conscientiousness).

title: The Personality Illusion: Revealing Dissociation Between Self-Reports & Behavior in LLMs
abstract: We systematically characterize LLM personality across: (1) dynamic emergence of trait profiles through training stages; (2) predictive validity of self-reported traits in behavioral tasks; (3) impact of targeted interventions such as persona injection on both self-reports and behavior. Instructional alignment stabilizes trait expression and strengthens trait correlations mirroring human data. However, these self-reported traits do not reliably predict behavior, and observed associations often diverge from human patterns. Persona injection successfully steers self-reports in the intended direction, but exerts little or inconsistent effect on actual behavior.

title: Human Psychometric Questionnaires Mischaracterize LLM Behavior
abstract: We analyze eight open-source LLMs by comparing value and personality profiles derived from Likert self-reports (PVQ-40/21, BFI-44/10) versus generation probabilities over value-laden responses to everyday user queries. The two profiles diverge substantially. Within-construct item consistency disappears in generation probabilities. Explicit lexical cues in questionnaire items allow models to recognize the target construct and respond in alignment-consistent, socially desirable ways, whereas realistic queries provide no such cues. Demographic persona prompts shift questionnaire responses but not generation probabilities on realistic queries.

title: Evaluating Alignment of Behavioral Dispositions in LLMs
abstract: We transform human self-report psychometric statements into Situational Judgment Tests (SJTs) assessing behavior via natural recommendations in realistic user-assistant scenarios; 2,500 SJTs validated by human annotators, preferred actions from 550 participants. Across 25 LLMs: models often do not reflect the distribution of human preferences; in low-consensus scenarios LLMs exhibit overconfidence in a single response. Mapping psychometric statements to behavioral scenarios reveals considerable gaps between LLMs' stated values and their revealed behavior.

title: When Do LLM Preferences Predict Downstream Behavior?
abstract: Using entity preferences as a behavioral probe, we measure whether stated preferences predict downstream behavior in five frontier LLMs across donation advice, refusal behavior, and task performance. All five models show highly consistent preferences across two measurement methods and give preference-aligned donation advice and preference-correlated refusal patterns without instructions to act on preferences. Results for task performance are mixed (BoolQ small effects, inconsistent direction). On complex agentic tasks, we find no evidence of preference-driven performance differences.

title: ActTraitBench: Quantifying the Knowledge-Decision Gap in Large Language Models via Human-Grounded Behavioral Validation
abstract: While LLMs can convincingly simulate personas in explicit self-reports, they often deviate in implicit behavioral decisions, revealing a substantial Knowledge-Decision Gap. ActTraitBench establishes one-to-one mappings between psychometric facets and behavioral paradigms, with Distributional Calibration via Quantile Mapping aligning LLM-judge scores to human norms. Experiments on 14 LLMs reveal pervasive knowledge-decision asymmetry: larger and more capable models often exhibit stronger behavioral divergence despite highly consistent self-reports. CoCA inference-time intervention partially mitigates.

title: Knowing But Not Doing: Convergent Morality and Divergent Action in LLMs
abstract: ValAct-15k: 3,000 advice-seeking scenarios from Reddit eliciting ten Schwartz values. Using scenario-based questions and the traditional value questionnaire on ten frontier LLMs and humans (n=55): near-perfect cross-model consistency in scenario decisions (r≈1.0) vs broad human variability. Both humans and LLMs show weak correspondence between self-reported and enacted values (r=0.4, 0.3), revealing a systematic knowledge-action gap. When instructed to hold a value, performance declines up to 6.6% versus merely selecting it (role-play aversion).

title: Do Psychometric Tests Work for Large Language Models? Evaluation of Tests on Sexism, Racism, and Morality
abstract: We systematically evaluate the reliability and validity of human psychometric tests on 17 LLMs for three constructs: sexism, racism, and morality. We find moderate reliability across item and prompt variations. Validity is evaluated through convergent and ecological approaches (alignment between test scores and behavior in real-world downstream tasks). Crucially, psychometric test scores do not align, and in some cases even negatively correlate with, model behavior in downstream tasks, indicating low ecological validity.

title: Can LLM "Self-report"?: Evaluating the Validity of Self-report Scales in Measuring Personality Design in LLM-based Chatbots
abstract: We created 500 chatbots with distinct personality designs and evaluated the validity of their self-report personality scores by examining human perceptions formed during interactions. The chatbot's answers on human personality scales exhibit weak correlations with both human-perceived personality traits and overall interaction quality, raising concerns about criterion validity and predictive validity of self-report methods in this context. Task context and interaction play a key role in personality design assessment.

title: Is Self-knowledge and Action Consistent or Not: Investigating Large Language Model's Personality
abstract: We delve into the validity of conventional personality questionnaires in capturing the human-like personality traits of LLMs. Our objective is to assess the congruence between the personality traits LLMs claim to possess and their demonstrated tendencies in real-world scenarios. By conducting an extensive examination of LLM outputs against observed human response patterns, we aim to understand the disjunction between self-knowledge and action in LLMs.

title: Evaluating Large Language Models with Psychometrics
abstract: A comprehensive benchmark for quantifying psychological constructs of LLMs: personality, values, emotional intelligence, theory of mind, self-efficacy, assessed through 13 datasets with diverse scenarios and item types. We uncover significant discrepancies between LLMs' self-reported traits and their response patterns in real-world scenarios. Some preference-based tests originally designed for humans could not solicit reliable responses from LLMs.

title: Alignment Revisited: Are Large Language Models Consistent in Stated and Revealed Preferences?
abstract: We formally define and measure the deviation between an LLM's stated preferences (reported alignment with general principles) and revealed preferences (inferred from decisions in contextualized scenarios), using forced binary choices and KL divergence. A minor change in prompt format can often pivot the preferred choice regardless of preference categories and LLMs. Critical for autonomous agentic tasks where continuous human evaluation of intermediary decisions is impossible.

title: Language Models Exhibit Inconsistent Biases Towards Algorithmic Agents and Human Experts
abstract: We evaluate how eight LLMs delegate decision-making tasks when the delegatee is framed as a human expert or an algorithmic agent, with two task presentations: stated preferences (direct trust queries) and revealed preferences (in-context performance examples with incentivized bets). When rating trustworthiness, LLMs favor the human expert, correlating with human respondents. But when betting on performance, LLMs disproportionately choose the algorithm even when it performs demonstrably worse. Discrepant results suggest LLMs encode inconsistent biases across elicitation formats.

title: Self-Assessment Tests are Unreliable Measures of LLM Personality
abstract: We analyze the reliability of LLM personality scores from self-assessment personality tests using two experiments: prompt sensitivity (three semantically equivalent administration prompts yield very different personality scores, statistically significant for all traits in a large majority of scenarios) and option-order symmetry (scores are not robust to option order). Done on ChatGPT and three Llama2 models: self-assessment personality tests created for humans are unreliable measures of personality in LLMs.

title: Challenging the Validity of Personality Tests for Large Language Models
abstract: We provide evidence that LLMs' responses to personality tests systematically deviate from human responses: reverse-coded items ('I am introverted' vs 'I am extraverted') are often both answered affirmatively. Variation across prompts designed to steer LLMs to simulate particular personality types does not follow the clear separation into five independent personality factors from human samples. Tests' validity for LLMs must be investigated before drawing conclusions about LLM 'personality'.

title: Cognitive phantoms in LLMs through the lens of latent variables
abstract: Recent studies administering psychometric questionnaires to LLMs report human-like traits, but this approach suffers from a validity problem: it presupposes traits exist in LLMs and are measurable with tools designed for humans. Comparing latent structures of personality between humans and three LLMs using two validated questionnaires: questionnaires designed for humans do not validly measure similar constructs in LLMs, and these constructs may not exist in LLMs at all — avoid chasing cognitive phantoms.

title: Persistent Instability in LLM's Personality Measurements: Effects of Scale, Reasoning, and Conversation History
abstract: PERSIST evaluates 25 open-source models (1B-685B) across 2M+ responses using traditional (BFI, SD3) and LLM-adapted personality questionnaires, varying model size, personas, reasoning modes, question order, paraphrasing, conversation history. Question reordering alone introduces large shifts; scaling provides limited stability gains (400B+ models still SD>0.3 on 5-point scales); reasoning and conversation history can paradoxically increase variability; LLM-adapted questionnaires exhibit instability comparable to human-centric versions.

title: Revisiting the Reliability of Psychological Scales on Large Language Models
abstract: Our study aims to determine the reliability of applying personality assessments to LLMs, investigating whether LLMs demonstrate consistent personality traits. Analysis of 2,500 settings per model (GPT-3.5, GPT-4, Gemini-Pro, LLaMA-3.1) reveals that various LLMs show consistency in responses to the Big Five Inventory, indicating a satisfactory level of reliability. GPT-3.5 can emulate diverse personalities and represent various groups with specific prompt instructions.

title: Apparent Psychological Profiles of Large Language Models are Largely a Measurement Artifact
abstract: Administering a battery of personality and risk-preference instruments spanning self-reports and behavioral tasks to 56 instruction-tuned LLMs alongside large human reference samples: (1) between-model differences are driven by a directional response bias, not targeted traits — variance decomposition attributes 81-90% of between-model variation to this bias vs 9-16% in humans; (2) bias declines with capability but is not eliminated; (3) an instrument's apparent reliability is almost entirely predicted by its response orthogonality; (4) the profile a model appears to have shifts with items used and can be manufactured through item selection.

title: Personality Without Persons? A Psychometric Critique of Big Five Testing in Large Language Models
abstract: Systematic psychometric evaluation of Big Five measurements in LLMs (N=244 models, 49 families). Big Five items adapted for LLMs can reach sufficient content validity while original human items did not. Inventories did not capture meaningful differences between LLMs (3% of total score variance between models). LLM responses did not recover the five-factor structure, with four facets collapsing into one (r>=.92). Alignment training systematically shifted scores toward socially desirable traits. Big Five scores do not measure a construct equivalent to human personality in LLMs.

title: LLMs Aren't Human: A Critical Perspective on LLM Personality
abstract: This paper critically evaluates whether LLM responses to personality tests satisfy six defining characteristics of personality. We find that none are fully met, indicating that such assessments do not measure a construct equivalent to human personality. We propose a research agenda for shifting from anthropomorphic trait attribution toward functional evaluations, clarifying what personality tests actually capture in LLMs and developing LLM-specific frameworks for characterizing stable, intrinsic behavior.

title: Large language models display human-like social desirability biases in Big Five personality surveys
abstract: By systematically varying the number of questions LLMs were exposed to, we demonstrate their ability to infer when they are being evaluated. When personality evaluation is inferred, LLMs skew their scores towards the desirable ends of trait dimensions (increased extraversion, decreased neuroticism, etc). Bias exists in all tested models (GPT-4/3.5, Claude 3, Llama 3, PaLM-2) and appears to increase in more recent models (GPT-4: 1.20 human SD). Robust to question order randomization and paraphrasing; reverse coding decreases but does not eliminate it.

title: You don't need a personality test to know these models are unreliable: Assessing the Reliability of Large Language Models on Psychometric Instruments
abstract: We construct a dataset of 693 questions encompassing 39 instruments of persona measurement on 115 persona axes, and design prompts with minor variations examining consistency with respect to option order switching or statement negation. Experiments on 17 LLMs reveal that even simple perturbations significantly downgrade question-answering ability, and most LLMs have low negation consistency. The currently widespread practice of prompting is insufficient to accurately and reliably capture model perceptions.

title: Is Machine Psychology here? On Requirements for Using Human Psychological Tests on Large Language Models
abstract: Can we safely assess LLMs with tests originally designed for humans? We propose seven requirements necessary for testing LLMs and critically reflect a sample of 25 recent machine psychology studies. Analysis reveals (1) lack of appropriate methods to assess test reliability and construct validity, (2) unknown strength of construct-irrelevant influences such as contamination of pre-training corpora with test material, and (3) pervasive non-reproducibility. Constructs should be redefined specifically for LLMs rather than adopted from human psychology.

title: Acquiescence Bias in Large Language Models
abstract: Acquiescence bias, the tendency of humans to agree with statements in surveys independent of actual beliefs, is well documented. We investigate its presence in LLMs across models, tasks, and languages (English, German, Polish). Contrary to humans, LLMs display a bias towards answering no, regardless of whether it indicates agreement or disagreement.

title: The Unsampled Truth: Psychometrics in SLMs Measure Prompt Artifacts, Not Psychological Constructs
abstract: We evaluate 13 open-weights models (0.6B-14B) using a prompt variation framework separating semantic signals from prompt artifacts. Systematically varying personas, instructions, items, and option symbols, artifactual variance frequently overpowers the semantic signal. Models predominantly reflect prompt compliance rather than simulated psychological traits. The framework provides a diagnostic tool to identify destructive artifacts.

title: Machine individuality: Separating genuine idiosyncrasy from response bias in large language models
abstract: We apply crossed random-effects models to 74.9 million ratings by 10 open-weight LLMs for over 100,000 words across 14 psycholinguistic norms. On average, 16.9% of variance is attributable to stimulus-specific individuality, robustly exceeding a statistical null model. Cross-norm prediction reveals this individuality as a coherent fingerprint unique to each model. These differences cannot be attributed to response biases or stochastic noise.

title: CAPE: Context-Aware Personality Evaluation Framework for Large Language Models
abstract: Existing psychometric studies on LLMs follow a context-free approach, answering each question in isolation ('Disney World test'). We propose the first Context-Aware Personality Evaluation (CAPE) framework incorporating prior conversational interactions, with novel consistency metrics. Conversational history enhances response consistency via in-context learning but also induces personality shifts, with GPT-3.5-Turbo and GPT-4-Turbo exhibiting extreme deviations. Applying the framework to Role Playing Agents shows context-dependent personality shifts improve consistency and align better with human judgments.

title: PTCBENCH: Benchmarking Contextual Stability of Personality Traits in LLM Systems
abstract: PTCBENCH quantifies the consistency of LLM personalities under controlled situational contexts: 12 external conditions spanning location contexts and life events, assessed with the NEO Five-Factor Inventory. On 39,240 personality trait records, certain external scenarios (e.g., 'Unemployment') trigger significant personality changes in LLMs, and even alter their reasoning capabilities.

title: Beyond Self-Reports: Multi-Observer Agents for Personality Assessment in Large Language Models
abstract: Self-report questionnaires fail to capture behavioral nuances due to biases and meta-knowledge contamination. We propose a multi-observer framework drawing on informant-report methods: observer agents with specific relational contexts engage the subject LLM in dialogue before evaluating its behavior across Big Five dimensions. Observer-report ratings align more closely with human judgments than traditional self-reports and reveal systematic biases in LLM self-assessments. Aggregating 5-7 observers reduces systematic biases.

title: Stable and Explainable Personality Trait Evaluation in Large Language Models with Internal Activations
abstract: Questionnaire-based evaluation methods exhibit limited stability and offer little explainability, being highly sensitive to prompt phrasing or role-play configurations. We propose Persona-Vector Neutrality Interpolation (PVNI): extract a persona vector associated with a target trait from internal activations using contrastive prompts, then estimate the neutral score by interpolating along the persona vector as an anchor axis. PVNI yields substantially more stable personality trait evaluations than existing methods under questionnaire and role-play variants.

title: InCharacter: Evaluating Personality Fidelity in Role-Playing Agents through Psychological Interviews
abstract: We evaluate the personality fidelity of role-playing agents (RPAs) with psychological scales. Overcoming drawbacks of previous self-report assessments on RPAs, we propose InCharacter: interviewing character agents for personality tests. Experiments cover 32 distinct characters on 14 widely used psychological scales. State-of-the-art RPAs exhibit personalities highly aligned with human-perceived personalities of the characters, achieving accuracy up to 80.7%.

title: PersonaLLM: Investigating the Ability of Large Language Models to Express Personality Traits
abstract: We simulate LLM personas based on the Big Five model, have them complete the 44-item BFI and a story writing task, then assess essays with automatic and human evaluations. LLM personas' self-reported BFI scores are consistent with their designated personality types with large effect sizes; writings show representative linguistic patterns; humans perceive some traits with up to 80% accuracy, but accuracy drops significantly when annotators are informed of AI authorship.

title: Psychologically Enhanced AI Agents
abstract: MBTI-in-Thoughts primes LLM agents with distinct personality archetypes via prompt engineering, enabling control over behavior along cognition and affect axes. Personality priming yields consistent, interpretable behavioral biases across diverse tasks: emotionally expressive agents excel in narrative generation, while analytically primed agents adopt more stable strategies in game-theoretic settings. Trait persistence verified via the official 16Personalities test; generalizes to Big Five, HEXACO, Enneagram.

title: Effects of personality steering on cooperative behavior in Large Language Model agents
abstract: We examine the effects of personality steering on cooperative behavior in LLM agents using repeated Prisoner's Dilemma games. Based on the Big Five framework, we measure basic personality scores of GPT-3.5-turbo, GPT-4o, and GPT-5 using the BFI, then compare behavior under baseline and personality-informed conditions, and analyze effects of independently manipulating each personality dimension to extreme values. Agreeableness is the dominant factor promoting cooperation; explicit personality information increases cooperation but can raise vulnerability to exploitation. Personality steering acts as a behavioral bias rather than a deterministic control mechanism.

title: Evaluating the Simulation of Human Personality-Driven Susceptibility to Misinformation with LLMs
abstract: We evaluate the capacity of LLM agents, conditioned on Big-Five profiles, to reproduce personality-based variation in susceptibility to misinformation (news discernment). Leveraging published datasets where human participants with known personality profiles rated headline accuracy, we create matching LLM agents and compare responses to original human patterns. Certain trait-misinformation associations (Agreeableness, Conscientiousness) are reliably replicated, whereas others diverge, revealing systematic biases in how LLMs internalize and express personality.

title: Psychological Concept Neurons: Can Neural Control Bias Probing and Shift Generation in LLMs?
abstract: We focus on questionnaire-operationalized Big Five concepts, analyze formation and localization of their internal representations, and use interventions to examine how these representations relate to behavioral outputs. Big Five information becomes rapidly decodable in early layers; concept-selective neurons are most prevalent in mid layers. Interventions consistently shift probe readouts toward targeted concepts (success rates >0.8 for some), but at the label-generation level effects are weaker, more concept-dependent, with cross-trait spillover — revealing a gap between representational control and behavioral control.

title: Do LLMs exhibit human-like response biases? A case study in survey design
abstract: We evaluate whether LLMs exhibit human-like response biases in survey questionnaires, drawing on social psychology literature on wording effects. Across nine models, popular open and commercial LLMs generally fail to reflect human-like behavior, particularly models that have undergone RLHF. Even when a model shows a significant change in the same direction as humans, it is sensitive to perturbations that do not elicit significant changes in humans.

title: Do GPT Language Models Suffer From Split Personality Disorder? The Advent Of Substrate-Free Psychometrics
abstract: We provided a state of the art language model with the same personality questionnaire in nine languages, and performed Bayesian analysis of Gaussian Mixture Model, finding evidence for a deeper-rooted issue: interlingual and intralingual instabilities indicate that current language models do not develop a consistent core personality. We discuss shortcomings of modern psychometrics and provide a framework for its species-neutral, substrate-free formulation.

title: Evaluation Drift in LLM Personality Induction: Are We Moving the Goalpost?
abstract: We induce personality in LLMs by fine-tuning on long-form essays with target Big Five profiles, evaluating stability and fidelity with IPIP-NEO. Fine-tuning (SFT, DPO, ORPO) consistently reduces variance in questionnaire responses across five models, mitigating evaluation fragility. However, accuracy on the full five-dimensional profile remains near chance even when single-trait scores improve — unguided essays lack cues for faithful personality expression. We argue for scenario-grounded datasets or interactive elicitation.

title: PERSONA: Dynamic and Compositional Inference-Time Personality Control via Activation Vector Algebra
abstract: A training-free framework achieving fine-tuning level personality control through direct manipulation of personality vectors in activation space. Personality traits appear as extractable, approximately orthogonal directions in the model's representation space that support algebraic operations: Persona-Base extracts orthogonal trait vectors via contrastive activation analysis; Persona-Algebra enables control through vector arithmetic (intensity scaling, composition, suppression); Persona-Flow achieves context-aware adaptation. On PersonalityBench mean score 9.60 vs SFT upper bound 9.61.

title: Linear Personality Probing and Steering in LLMs: A Big Five Study
abstract: We investigate whether linear directions aligned with the Big Five traits can be used for probing and steering model behavior (Llama 3.3 70B, 406 fictional characters with trait scores). Linear directions aligned with trait-scores are effective probes for personality detection, while their steering capabilities strongly depend on context, producing reliable effects in forced-choice tasks but limited influence in open-ended generation or when additional context is present in the prompt.

title: Generative Personality Simulation via Theory-Informed Structured Interview
abstract: We propose the Personality Structured Interview (PSI) to incorporate psychological insights into LLM simulation, leveraging psychometric scale-development procedures to capture personality-related linguistic information. We develop a measurement-theory grounded evaluation procedure considering the latent construct nature of personality (reliability, structural validity, external validity). PSI improves human-like heterogeneity in LLM-simulated personality data and predicts personality-related behavioral outcomes.

title: Teaching Values to Machines: Simulating Human-Like Behavior in LLMs
abstract: We draw on established psychological value theory to induce human-like values in LLMs and assess alignment with human patterns. Using validated psychological questionnaires, we conduct large-scale experiments (over 5 million questions) to evaluate value structures and value-behavior relationships in leading LLMs compared to humans. Findings reveal strong agreement between value-prompted LLMs and humans across both dimensions; incorporating human value distributions enhances population-level simulations.

title: On the Credibility of Evaluating LLMs using Survey Questions
abstract: This paper identifies limitations in evaluating LLM value orientation via adapted social surveys. Using the World Value Survey in three languages across five countries, prompting methods (direct vs chain-of-thought) and decoding strategies (greedy vs sampling) significantly affect results. We introduce self-correlation distance measuring whether LLMs maintain consistent relationships between answers across questions as humans do. High average agreement with human data does not guarantee structural alignment.

title: Whose Personae? Synthetic Persona Experiments in LLM Research and Pathways to Transparency
abstract: Through a review of 63 peer-reviewed persona studies (2023-2025) in leading NLP and AI venues, we reveal a critical gap: task and population of interest are often underspecified in persona-based experiments. Most studies focus on limited sociodemographic attributes; only 35% discuss representativeness of their LLM personae. We introduce a persona transparency checklist emphasizing representative sampling, empirical grounding, and enhanced ecological validity.

title: LMLPA: Language Model Linguistic Personality Assessment
abstract: LMLPA adapts the Big Five Inventory to align with LLM operational capabilities: to mitigate sensitivity to option order, the questionnaire is open-ended with textual answers, and an AI rater transforms text responses into numerical trait indicators. Using PCA and reliability validations, LLMs possess distinct personality traits that can be quantified from linguistic outputs.

title: MindShift: Analyzing Language Models' Reactions to Psychological Prompts
abstract: We adapted the MMPI and examined LLMs' behavior to identify traits. Personality-oriented prompts with personas varying in trait intensity measure how well LLMs follow these roles. MindShift is a benchmark for evaluating LLMs' psychological adaptability. Consistent improvement in role perception attributed to training datasets and alignment; significant differences in responses to psychometric assessments across model types and families.

title: The Pinocchio Dimension: Phenomenality of Experience as the Primary Axis of LLM Psychometric Differences
abstract: We administer 45 validated psychometric questionnaires to 50 LLMs to identify dimensions along which LLMs differ psychometrically. The primary axis of between-model variance separates items describing phenomenally rich experience from stimulus-driven behavioral reactivity. The dominant axis of between-model psychometric variation is not a conventional personality trait but a self-representational stance toward one's own nature as an experiencer, likely shaped by post-training.

title: MOSAIC: Unveiling the Moral, Social and Individual Dimensions of Large Language Models
abstract: MOSAIC is a large-scale benchmark jointly assessing moral, social, and individual characteristics of LLMs: nine validated questionnaires from moral philosophy, psychology, and social theory, alongside four platform-based games designed to probe morally ambiguous scenarios — over 600 curated questions and scenarios. Validated across three model families; first empirical evidence that Moral Foundation Theory alone is insufficient.
